#problem 1

```{r}
# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)   # For data manipulation, piping, and visualization

# Load the dataset from the .rds file
nzge <- readRDS("nzge.rds")

# Inspect the structure of the data (optional but good practice)
glimpse(nzge)
```

###a
```{r}
# Group by election year and voting type, then calculate total votes
nzge %>%
  group_by(election_year, voting_type) %>%
  summarise(
    total_votes = sum(votes, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"  # Drops grouping after summarise to avoid warnings
  ) %>%
  arrange(total_votes) %>%  # Sort by total votes in ascending order
  print(n = Inf)            # Print all rows
```

Code Logic: We use group_by() to separate the data by both election_year and voting_type (ensuring Candidate and Party votes are kept distinct). summarise() calculates the total sum of the votes column. arrange() sorts the resulting table.

Summary: The output shows that overall voter turnout (total votes cast) generally increased from 2002 to 2014. In every election year, there are slightly more Party votes cast than Candidate votes, which is typical as some voters may only cast a party vote.


###b
```{r}
# 筛选 2014 年、仅候选人票 (Candidate)
nzge %>%
  filter(election_year == 2014, voting_type == "Candidate") %>%
  group_by(party) %>%
  summarise(
    votes = sum(votes, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # 计算各党占候选人总票数的百分比
    percent = votes / sum(votes) * 100
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(percent)) %>%    # 按得票百分比降序排序
  print(n = Inf)
```


Code Logic: We use filter() to isolate the 2014 Candidate election data. After grouping by party and calculating the total votes, mutate() creates a new percent column by dividing each party's votes by the overall sum of votes. arrange(desc()) ranks them from highest to lowest.

Summary: In the 2014 Candidate election, the National Party won the majority of the votes with approximately 45.5%, followed by the Labour Party at 33.7%. The table also includes "Informal Candidate Votes" (invalid votes), which is a standard inclusion in New Zealand's official election data.


###c
```{r}
# Find the winning party for each year and vote type
nzge %>%
  # First, aggregate total votes per year, type, and party
  group_by(election_year, voting_type, party) %>%
  summarise(
    total_votes = sum(votes, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Then, group by year and type to find the top party
  group_by(election_year, voting_type) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = total_votes, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Keep only relevant columns and reshape the data
  select(election_year, voting_type, party) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from   = voting_type,
    values_from  = party,
    names_prefix = "Winner_"
  ) %>%
  arrange(election_year) %>%
  print(n = Inf)
```

Code Logic: We first calculate total votes per party per year per type. Then, slice_max() isolates the row with the highest votes for each election_year and voting_type. with_ties = FALSE ensures only one winner is returned. Finally, pivot_wider() reshapes the data so that the Candidate and Party winners are displayed side-by-side for each year.

Summary: The table reveals a major political shift in New Zealand. From 2002 to 2005, the Labour Party dominated the Party vote. However, starting in 2008, the National Party secured both the Candidate and Party votes and maintained this dominance through 2014. Interestingly, in 2005, the National Party won the most Candidate votes, but the Labour Party won the overall Party vote—a great example of how New Zealand's MMP (Mixed-Member Proportional) electoral system works.


Through this analysis using tidyverse and dplyr, we successfully separated and analyzed Candidate and Party votes in New Zealand's general elections. We observed that total votes have grown over time. Looking specifically at 2014, the National Party held a strong lead in Candidate votes. Furthermore, our year-by-year winner analysis highlighted the transition of power from Labour to National in 2008, and captured the nuanced 2005 election where the two vote types produced different winning parties. The use of piping (%>%) and modern dplyr functions ensured the code was readable, efficient, and free of deprecated functions.


#problem 2
```{r}
# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
#install.packages("infer")
library(infer) # For Hypothesis Testing (Q3)

# Read the data directly from the web (Raw link)
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/azhou5849/tennis-atp-sackmann-data/master/atp_matches_2019.csv"
atp <- read_csv(url)
```

###a
```{r}
# Count distinct tournament IDs
tournament_count <- atp %>%
  distinct(tourney_id) %>%
  count()

print(tournament_count)
```
There were 128 tournaments that took place in 2019.

###b
```{r}
# Find the winners: Filter for the Final match of each tournament
tournament_winners <- atp %>%
  filter(round == "F") %>%
  distinct(tourney_id, winner_name)

# Count how many titles each player won
win_counts <- tournament_winners %>%
  count(winner_name, sort = TRUE)

# Find how many players won >1 tournament and the maximum number of wins
multiple_winners_summary <- win_counts %>%
  filter(n > 1) %>%
  summarise(
    players_with_multiple = n(),
    max_titles = max(n)
  )

print(multiple_winners_summary)

# See who won the most
print(win_counts %>% filter(n == max(n)))
```
12 players won more than one tournament in 2019. The most winning players were Dominic Thiem and Novak Djokovic, who each won 5 tournaments.


###c
```{r}
library(infer)

# 1. Reshape the data to a long format to compare Winners and Losers
ace_data <- atp %>%
  filter(!is.na(w_ace) & !is.na(l_ace)) %>%
  select(match_num, w_ace, l_ace) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(w_ace, l_ace),
    names_to = "role",
    values_to = "aces"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    role = if_else(role == "w_ace", "Winner", "Loser")
  )

# 2. Calculate the observed difference in means
observed_diff <- ace_data %>%
  group_by(role) %>%
  summarise(mean_aces = mean(aces)) %>%
  summarise(diff = mean_aces[role == "Winner"] - mean_aces[role == "Loser"]) %>%
  pull(diff)

# 3. Permutation Test using the 'infer' package
set.seed(123)
null_dist <- ace_data %>%
  specify(response = aces, explanatory = role) %>%
  hypothesize(null = "independence") %>%
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") %>%
  calculate(stat = "diff in means", order = c("Winner", "Loser"))

# 4. Calculate p-value
p_value <- null_dist %>%
  summarise(p_value = mean(stat >= observed_diff)) %>%
  pull(p_value)


print(paste("Observed difference:", round(observed_diff, 2)))

print(paste("P-value:", round(p_value, 4)))

```

Yes, there is strong evidence. The observed difference in means is 1.7, meaning winners hit an average of 1.7 more aces per match than losers. The permutation test yielded a p-value of 0 (or < 0.001), indicating this difference is highly statistically significant.


###d
```{r}
# Reshape the data to a long format
player_winrate <- atp %>%
  select(winner_name, loser_name) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(winner_name, loser_name), 
               names_to = "role", 
               values_to = "player") %>%
  mutate(won = if_else(role == "winner_name", 1, 0)) %>%
  group_by(player) %>%
  summarise(
    matches = n(),
    wins = sum(won),
    win_rate = wins / matches,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(matches >= 5) %>% 
  arrange(desc(win_rate))

print(player_winrate %>% slice_max(win_rate))
```
Among players with at least 5 matches, Rafael Nadal had the highest win rate. He played 69 matches, won 60, and achieved a win rate of 87.0%.


#problem 3

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)   
library(scales)    

#read data
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nytimes/covid-19-data/refs/heads/master/rolling-averages/us-states.csv"
covid_data <- read_csv(url, show_col_types = FALSE)

us_states <- state.name
covid_clean <- covid_data %>%
  filter(state %in% c(us_states, "District of Columbia"))
```

###a
```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "National COVID-19 Case Trajectory: 7-day rolling average of new cases, highlighting major and minor spikes."

library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
library(scales)

# 1. Calculate the national daily average
national_data <- covid_clean %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(national_avg = sum(cases_avg, na.rm = TRUE))

# 2. Find the maximum peak for label positioning
max_cases <- max(national_data$national_avg, na.rm = TRUE)

# 3. Create a data frame for the labels
label_data <- tibble(
  date = as.Date(c("2021-01-11", "2021-08-25", "2022-01-11", "2020-07-15", "2021-04-15")),
  y_pos = c(max_cases * 0.7, max_cases * 0.5, max_cases * 0.8, max_cases * 0.3, max_cases * 0.3),
  label = c("Major Spike 1\n(Winter 2020-21)", "Major Spike 2\n(Delta)", "Major Spike 3\n(Omicron)", 
            "Minor Spike\n(Summer 2020)", "Minor Spike\n(Spring 2021)"),
  type = c("Major", "Major", "Major", "Minor", "Minor")
)

# 4. Plot the trajectory
p1 <- ggplot(national_data, aes(x = date, y = national_avg)) +
  geom_area(fill = "#2c7fb8", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(color = "#253494", linewidth = 0.8) +
  
  # Add vertical lines
  geom_vline(xintercept = label_data$date[label_data$type == "Major"], 
             linetype = "dashed", color = "red", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = label_data$date[label_data$type == "Minor"], 
             linetype = "dotted", color = "orange", linewidth = 0.8) +
  
  # Add labels using ggrepel to avoid overlapping
  geom_text_repel(
    data = label_data,
    aes(x = date, y = y_pos, label = label, color = type),
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 4.5,
    nudge_x = 20,         
    direction = "y",      
    box.padding = 0.8,    
    force = 2,            
    min.segment.length = 0, 
    segment.color = "grey50",
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  
  # Formatting
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Major" = "red", "Minor" = "darkorange")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %Y", date_breaks = "4 months") +
  
  labs(
    title = "National COVID-19 Case Trajectory",
    subtitle = "7-day rolling average of new cases, highlighting major and minor spikes",
    x = NULL, 
    y = "Daily New Cases (7-Day Average)",
    caption = "Data Source: NYTimes COVID-19 Data"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

print(p1)
```
Code Logic (Q1): To visualize the national trend, I aggregated the data using group_by(date) and summarise(sum()) to get the total US daily average. I then used geom_vline and annotate to manually highlight the distinct peaks. The ggrepel package was used for the text labels to prevent overlapping, ensuring the graph is publication-ready.

By observing the national 7-day average, we can identify three major spikes and several minor spikes in COVID-19 cases.

The major spikes align with distinct variant-driven waves: the Winter 2020-2021 surge, the Delta variant (Fall 2021), and the massive Omicron variant (Winter 2022). The minor spikes occurred during the Summer of 2020 and Spring of 2021.

This visualization supports the argument that COVID-19 transmission was not a single continuous outbreak, but rather occurred in distinct, variant-driven waves separated by periods of relative decline.


###b
```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Trajectory Comparison: Highest vs. Lowest Overall Rates. The x-axis shows time, and the y-axis shows the 7-day average cases per 100k."

# 1. Calculate the overall rate for each state and identify the extremes
state_overall <- covid_clean %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  summarise(total_rate = sum(cases_avg_per_100k, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  arrange(desc(total_rate))

highest_state <- state_overall$state[1]
lowest_state <- state_overall$state[nrow(state_overall)]

# 2. Filter data for only these two states
top_bottom_data <- covid_clean %>%
  filter(state %in% c(highest_state, lowest_state))

# 3. Create the plot
p2 <- ggplot(top_bottom_data, aes(x = date, y = cases_avg_per_100k, color = state)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  
  # Use distinct colors for the highest and lowest states
  scale_color_manual(values = setNames(c("#e31a1c", "#1f78b4"), c(highest_state, lowest_state))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %Y", date_breaks = "6 months") +
  
  # Formatting for publication
  labs(
    title = "Trajectory Comparison: Highest vs. Lowest Overall Rates",
    subtitle = paste("Highest Rate State:", highest_state, "| Lowest Rate State:", lowest_state),
    x = NULL,
    y = "Cases per 100k (7-Day Average)",
    color = "State"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = c(0.15, 0.85), # Place legend in the top-left empty space
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "black")
  )

print(p2)
```
Code Logic (Q2): I calculated the total cumulative rate for each state using sum(cases_avg_per_100k) and sorted them to find the absolute highest and lowest. I then filtered the dataset for just these two states (filter(state %in% c(highest_state, lowest_state))) and plotted their trajectories on the same time scale to visually compare their peak timing and magnitude.

The state with the highest overall rate (Rhode Island) and the state with the lowest overall rate (Maine) show highly synchronized trajectories in terms of timing, but massive differences in magnitude.

Both states experienced their major peaks at roughly the same times (e.g., Winter 2020-21, the Delta wave in late 2021, and the Omicron wave in Winter 2022). This synchronization strongly suggests that national or global events (such as holiday travel and the emergence of new variants) drove the timing of the waves across the country.

However, Rhode Island's peaks are drastically taller than Maine's, particularly during the Omicron surge where Rhode Island peaked at over 500 cases per 100k compared to Maine's ~80 cases per 100k. This indicates that while the timing was dictated by national trends, local factors—such as population density or state-level public health policies—played a crucial role in amplifying the absolute impact of each wave.


###c
```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "The First Five States to Experience Substantial COVID-19 Spread. The dots indicate the exact date the state crossed the threshold of 1 case per 100k."

# 1. Identify the first five states to cross the 1 case/100k threshold
early_2020 <- covid_clean %>%
  filter(date <= as.Date("2020-06-30")) %>%
  filter(cases_avg_per_100k >= 1) %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  summarise(first_date = min(date)) %>%
  arrange(first_date) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)

# 2. Filter data for these five states
first_five_data <- covid_clean %>%
  filter(state %in% early_2020$state, date <= as.Date("2020-06-30"))

# 3. Plot the trajectories
p3 <- ggplot(first_five_data, aes(x = date, y = cases_avg_per_100k, color = state)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  
  # Mark the threshold points
  geom_point(data = early_2020, aes(x = first_date, y = 1), size = 3, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  
  # Formatting
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "1 month") +
  labs(
    title = "The First Five States to Experience Substantial COVID-19 Spread",
    subtitle = "Substantial spread defined as reaching a 7-day average of 1 case per 100k",
    x = "Date (Early 2020)",
    y = "Cases per 100k (7-Day Average)",
    color = "State", 
    caption = "Dots indicate the exact date the state crossed the threshold."
  ) +
  theme_light(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right", 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

print(p3)
```
Code Logic: To test if winners hit more aces than losers, I used a Permutation Test via the infer package, strictly adhering to the Tidyverse ecosystem. Because infer requires a categorical explanatory variable for a difference in means, I used pivot_longer to reshape the data so that the "role" (Winner vs. Loser) became a categorical variable. I generated 1000 null distributions by permuting the labels to calculate the p-value.

By defining "substantial spread" as crossing the threshold of a 1 case per 100k rolling average, the data clearly shows that the earliest states affected were primarily major coastal and travel hubs.

The plot highlights that District of Columbia, Louisiana, New Jersey, New York, and Washington crossed the threshold almost simultaneously in mid-March 2020 (indicated by the black dots). However, shortly after this initial milestone, New York (the purple line) experienced an explosive, vertical surge, peaking at over 50 cases per 100k—far outpacing the other early states.

This aligns with historical context: the initial wave of infections was heavily driven by international travel and dense urban centers. While states like Washington saw early cases due to travel from Asia, New York's massive spike was driven by travel from Europe, disproportionately impacting the East Coast before the virus spread inland.
